blocks.source: Vol III, Multi-Agent Coordination, § Historical Perspective and Further Reading
blocks.md: The question of when dividing computational work yields a net speedup is older than autonomous software agents. Gene Amdahl's 1967 argument established that serial execution fractions strictly cap the speedup achievable by adding processors. Two years later, Ronald Graham showed that while greedy list scheduling lands close to the theoretical dependency bound, adding parallel resources can paradoxically increase total completion time. Neil Gunther later unified these dynamics in the universal scalability law, introducing a pairwise coherency penalty to explain how crosstalk and contention turn throughput saturation into outright performance collapse.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Amdahl's law matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: For a fixed amount of work with no coordination overhead, the serial fraction 1-p caps speedup at 1/(1-p) however many workers are added, and the universal scalability law reduces to it when coherency is zero.

questions.q: The section **Historical Perspective and Further Reading** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: For a fixed amount of work with no coordination overhead, the serial fraction 1-p caps speedup at 1/(1-p) however many workers are added, and the universal scalability law reduces to it when coherency is zero.
The dependency graph, the communication topology, and the supervision tree are separate structures, and conflating them hides quadratic communication cost and orphaned lifecycles.

Shared working directories produce lost updates and torn reads, and write sets collide with probability 1 - exp(-N(N-1)w^2/2F), so isolation is provided per worker and a merge is validated, not trusted.

Delegation is justified only if it beats a capable single controller on the same tasks, criteria, evidence access, concurrency, and resource ceilings, scored on end-to-end acceptance with every initiated task counted.
